situation: Priest at the ghat catches your hand and presses flower petals into it, starting an unrequested puja
say: मुझे अभी पूजा नहीं करनी, माफ़ कीजिए।
roman: Mujhe abhi puja nahi karni, maaf kijiye.
means: I don't want to do puja right now, sorry.
why: Stated as your own decision, not a question - a question like 'kya main karu?' invites him to keep persuading, a flat statement doesn't.

situation: He keeps pushing flowers into your hand and won't let go, still in the polite phase
say: हाथ छोड़िए, मुझे नहीं करनी पूजा।
roman: Haath chhodiye, mujhe nahi karni puja.
means: Let go of my hand, I don't want to do the puja.
why: Names the actual physical act - haath chhodiye, let go of my hand - so he has to respond to the touch itself, which is the real violation, not just the refusal.

situation: He still won't let go or stop after the polite refusal - moving firmer
say: मैंने मना कर दिया है, अब हाथ छोड़िए वरना मैं शोर मचाऊँगी।
roman: Maine mana kar diya hai, ab haath chhodiye warna main shor machaungi.
means: I have already refused, let go now or I will start shouting.
why: States the refusal as an already-completed fact, removing his opening to keep asking, and names the consequence before doing it, which alone often ends it.

situation: Signalling you are Indian and already know the ghat routine, so the price and pressure drop instantly
say: मैं यहीं की हूँ, ये सब पता है मुझे, रेट मत बढ़ाइए।
roman: Main yahin ki hoon, ye sab pata hai mujhe, rate mat badhaiye.
means: I'm from here, I already know all this, don't inflate the rate.
why: This exact combination - yahin ki hoon plus ye sab pata hai - is the line that flips you from tourist-tariff to local-tariff, because it tells him the foreigner script won't work on you.

situation: Priest demands money after a puja you never actually agreed to
say: मैंने पूजा करने के लिए हाँ नहीं कहा था, मैं पैसे नहीं दूँगी।
roman: Maine puja karne ke liye haan nahi kaha tha, main paise nahi doongi.
means: I never said yes to this puja, I will not pay.
why: Argues from consent, not price - the whole scam depends on treating an unrequested act as a billable service, so refusing on consent grounds closes the argument instead of opening a haggle.

situation: A red thread (mauli) has already been tied on your wrist and a donation is being asked per family member
say: ये धागा मैंने बंधवाने को नहीं कहा था, मैं सिर्फ़ इतना ही दूँगी।
roman: Ye dhaaga maine bandhwane ko nahi kaha tha, main sirf itna hi doongi.
means: I didn't ask for this thread to be tied, I'll only give this much.
why: Names your own ceiling before he can multiply it by counting family members - stopping the per-head math is easier than arguing against it once it starts.

situation: He insists on separate donation amounts per family member you mention or he counts
say: परिवार के नाम पर अलग-अलग पैसे नहीं चलेंगे, एक ही दान है।
roman: Parivar ke naam par alag-alag paise nahi chalenge, ek hi daan hai.
means: Separate money per family member won't work, there is only one donation.
why: Names the mechanism itself - per-person counting - instead of just repeating no; saying what the trick is often makes someone drop it because they know you've clocked it.

situation: He threatens that removing the red thread is bad luck, to pressure more money
say: धागा अपनी जगह रहेगा, पैसे इतने ही मिलेंगे।
roman: Dhaaga apni jagah rahega, paise itne hi milenge.
means: The thread stays where it is, the money will only be this much.
why: Decouples the two things he's bundling - you keep the thread he was using as leverage while refusing more money, which takes the point out of the bad-luck threat.

situation: Auto driver quotes an obviously tripled fare for a short distance
say: इतना ज़्यादा नहीं चलता यहाँ, सही रेट बताइए।
roman: Itna zyada nahi chalta yahan, sahi rate bataiye.
means: It doesn't cost this much here, tell me the correct rate.
why: Signals local knowledge without naming a number first - whoever states a number first anchors the negotiation, so make him move first.

situation: Making your counter-offer after his inflated quote
say: मैं तीस रुपए दूँगी, चलना है तो बताइए।
roman: Main tees rupaye doongi, chalna hai to bataiye.
means: I will give thirty rupees, tell me if you want to go.
why: Framed as a final number with a yes/no attached, not an opening bid he can negotiate up from - this avoids the back-and-forth that usually lands in his favour.

situation: Walking away when the driver won't come down to a fair price
say: ठीक है, कोई और मिल जाएगा।
roman: Theek hai, koi aur mil jaayega.
means: Fine, I'll find someone else.
why: Only works said while actually turning to walk - the line just narrates the leverage, which is removing his sense that you need this exact auto right now.

situation: Agreeing the total fare for a camel ride, before mounting
say: पूरे राइड का कुल कितना होगा, अभी बता दीजिए।
roman: Poore ride ka kul kitna hoga, abhi bata dijiye.
means: Tell me right now what the total for the whole ride will be.
why: Asking for the kul (grand total) blocks the common move of quoting per-person or per-leg and adding waiting or return charges once you're already mounted and can't easily get off.

situation: Agreeing the duration of the camel ride, before mounting
say: कितनी देर की सवारी है ये, टाइम बता दीजिए।
roman: Kitni der ki sawaari hai ye, time bata dijiye.
means: How long is this ride, tell me the time.
why: Price and duration are sold together verbally but drift apart in practice - asking duration as its own question stops a promised half hour quietly becoming ten minutes.

situation: Agreeing headcount for the camel ride before mounting, so a child or extra person isn't billed separately later
say: हम कुल कितने लोग बैठेंगे, इसी रेट में सब आएँगे?
roman: Hum kul kitne log baithenge, isi rate mein sab aayenge?
means: How many of us total will sit, will everyone be included in this same rate?
why: Forces the per-head clause into the open before mounting - it's usually announced only at the end of the ride, when you have no bargaining position left.

situation: Closing the camel-ride price conversation before mounting, so nothing changes mid-ride
say: पहले तय कर लेते हैं, बाद में कोई एक्स्ट्रा पैसे नहीं दूँगी।
roman: Pehle tay kar lete hain, baad mein koi extra paise nahi doongi.
means: Let's fix it now, I won't pay anything extra later.
why: Said before mounting, while you still have full ability to walk away - the same sentence mid-ride carries no force because you're now on the animal in open desert.

situation: An unsolicited 'guide' attaches himself and starts walking alongside you
say: मुझे गाइड नहीं चाहिए, आप जाइए।
roman: Mujhe guide nahi chahiye, aap jaiye.
means: I don't need a guide, please go.
why: Aap jaiye is a direct instruction to leave, not just a statement of preference - a statement alone he can pretend not to have heard as a no.

situation: The guide keeps following after already being told no once
say: मैंने बोल दिया न, मुझे साथ नहीं चाहिए, पीछा मत कीजिए।
roman: Maine bol diya na, mujhe saath nahi chahiye, peecha mat kijiye.
means: I already told you, I don't want company, stop following me.
why: Names the specific act - peecha mat kijiye, don't follow - which is harder to shrug off than repeating a general no.

situation: A guide claims a guide or permission is required to enter a temple or ghat area, which usually isn't true
say: यहाँ जाने के लिए गाइड ज़रूरी नहीं है, मुझे पता है।
roman: Yahan jaane ke liye guide zaroori nahi hai, mujhe pata hai.
means: A guide isn't required to go here, I already know that.
why: Contradicts the false claim directly instead of just declining the offer, which stops him repeating the same line to the next person while you're still standing there.

situation: Shopkeeper opens at roughly three times the real price
say: इतना नहीं, आधे से भी कम में बताइए।
roman: Itna nahi, aadhe se bhi kam mein bataiye.
means: Not this much, quote less than half.
why: Anchors below half immediately instead of nibbling down from his number - the standard opening move against an opening bid that's already three times real value.

situation: Mid-bargain, shopkeeper has come down a little but not enough
say: थोड़ा और कम कीजिए, तभी लूँगी।
roman: Thoda aur kam kijiye, tabhi loongi.
means: Bring it down a bit more, only then will I take it.
why: Tabhi loongi ties the price drop directly to the sale happening, making the discount feel like it earns him the deal rather than something given away for nothing.

situation: Shopkeeper claims the current price is already final
say: ये फाइनल नहीं है, यहाँ का असली रेट मुझे पता है।
roman: Ye final nahi hai, yahan ka asli rate mujhe pata hai.
means: This isn't final, I know the real local rate here.
why: Asli rate pata hai is the single phrase that tells him you're not guessing - the exact line that changes how he negotiates from that point.

situation: Final step in the bargaining ladder - walking away to force a real price drop
say: रहने दीजिए, इतने में नहीं लूँगी।
roman: Rehne dijiye, itne mein nahi loongi.
means: Leave it, I won't take it at this price.
why: Said while turning away, not as another bid - it changes the question from how low will you go to do you want this sale at all, which is what actually moves a stuck price.

situation: Confirming the agreed price out loud before handing over money
say: तो पक्का इतने में हुआ, है ना?
roman: To pakka itne mein hua, hai na?
means: So it's confirmed at this price, right?
why: Said in front of shop staff or other customers nearby, a verbal confirmation on record makes a last-second price bump much harder to pull once money is out.

situation: Checking whether a lassi, cookie or sweet has bhang in it before eating or drinking
say: इसमें भांग तो नहीं है ना? मुझे नहीं चाहिए।
roman: Isme bhaang to nahi hai na? Mujhe nahi chahiye.
means: This doesn't have bhang in it, does it? I don't want it.
why: Phrased as a negative confirmation rather than an open question - an open 'kya isme kuch hai' can get a vague non-answer, this form is harder to dodge.

situation: Explicitly asking for the plain, non-bhang version at a shop that sells both openly
say: सादी लस्सी दीजिए, भांग वाली नहीं।
roman: Saadi lassi dijiye, bhaang waali nahi.
means: Give me the plain lassi, not the bhang one.
why: Names both options the way these shops actually menu them - many sell both side by side, so asking for the plain one by its own name gets a straight answer instead of relying on him to volunteer it.

situation: Checking a sweet or cookie at a stall known to sell bhang-laced items
say: क्या इसमें भांग मिली हुई है? साफ़-साफ़ बताइए।
roman: Kya isme bhaang mili hui hai? Saaf-saaf bataiye.
means: Is bhang mixed into this? Tell me clearly.
why: Saaf-saaf bataiye (tell me clearly) preempts the vague half-answer that lets a seller technically avoid lying without actually telling you.

situation: Ordering food and asking for no onion, no garlic
say: प्याज़-लहसुन बिल्कुल मत डालिए, बिना प्याज़-लहसुन का बनाइए।
roman: Pyaaz-lehsun bilkul mat daaliye, bina pyaaz-lehsun ka banaiye.
means: Don't put onion-garlic at all, make it without onion-garlic.
why: Repeats the request as both a prohibition and a cooking instruction - a single 'no onion garlic' is often heard as a preference and skipped under rush, restating it as how to cook it is taken more seriously.

situation: Asking for less oil in the food
say: तेल बहुत कम डालिएगा, हल्का बनाइए।
roman: Tel bahut kam daaliyega, halka banaiye.
means: Put very little oil, make it light.
why: Halka (light) is the actual word cooks use for low-oil food - it lands as a firmer instruction than a literal 'kam tel', which some cooks read as only a mild suggestion.

situation: Asking for less spicy food
say: मिर्च कम रखिए, बहुत तीखा मत बनाइए।
roman: Mirch kam rakhiye, bahut teekha mat banaiye.
means: Keep the chili low, don't make it very spicy.
why: Names both the ingredient (mirch) and the end quality (teekha) - a cook who hears only 'kam masala' may still load chili, since masala and mirch aren't the same axis in Rajasthani cooking.

situation: Asking specifically for Jain food, which excludes root vegetables entirely
say: जैन खाना चाहिए, प्याज़-लहसुन और आलू भी नहीं।
roman: Jain khaana chahiye, pyaaz-lehsun aur aalu bhi nahi.
means: I need Jain food, no onion-garlic and no potato either.
why: Naming Jain khaana invokes a whole recognized category most Rajasthani cooks already know, instead of you listing every excluded vegetable yourself.

situation: Asking a shop or hotel to hold your luggage for the day
say: क्या आप मेरा सामान थोड़ी देर के लिए रख सकते हैं?
roman: Kya aap mera saamaan thodi der ke liye rakh sakte hain?
means: Can you keep my luggage for a little while?
why: Phrased as a favour-sized request rather than a formal cloakroom ask, which matches how small Pushkar shops actually hold bags informally for customers.

situation: Asking what it costs to have luggage held, before handing it over
say: इसके लिए पैसे लगेंगे क्या?
roman: Iske liye paise lagenge kya?
means: Will there be a charge for this?
why: Asked before the bag goes behind his counter, not after - once it's already there you have no position to dispute whatever price he names at pickup.

situation: Asking to use a bathroom inside a shop or restaurant
say: क्या यहाँ वॉशरूम है? इस्तेमाल कर सकती हूँ?
roman: Kya yahan washroom hai? Istemaal kar sakti hoon?
means: Is there a washroom here? Can I use it?
why: The two-part ask gets past shops that don't advertise a washroom but will still let a customer use one if asked directly and politely.

situation: Asking for the nearest public toilet on the street
say: आस-पास कोई सुलभ शौचालय है क्या?
roman: Aas-paas koi sulabh shauchalay hai kya?
means: Is there a Sulabh toilet nearby?
why: Sulabh Shauchalay is the actual name of India's public-toilet chain, so naming it gets a precise direction instead of a vague wave toward general facilities.

situation: Asking for directions in an unfamiliar market, deliberately choosing to ask a woman
say: बहनजी, ज़रा रास्ता बता दीजिए, ...(जगह) कैसे जाऊँ?
roman: Behanji, zara raasta bata dijiye, ...(jagah) kaise jaaun?
means: Sister, please tell me the way, how do I get to ...(place)?
why: Opening with behanji, a respectful address used specifically for women, both signals who you're speaking to and defaults you to asking a woman or a family group first, the safer choice in an unfamiliar market.

situation: Asking a woman specifically for help when you feel unsafe or think someone is following you
say: दीदी, मुझे थोड़ी मदद चाहिए, कोई पीछे आ रहा है।
roman: Didi, mujhe thodi madad chahiye, koi peeche aa raha hai.
means: Sister, I need a little help, someone is following me.
why: Didi plus the exact problem in one breath gets a woman bystander to act fast, since specificity is what turns a stranger into actual help rather than sympathy.

situation: Someone won't leave you alone - step one, staying polite
say: माफ़ कीजिए, मुझे अकेले रहना है, आप जाइए।
roman: Maaf kijiye, mujhe akele rehna hai, aap jaiye.
means: Excuse me, I want to be alone, please go.
why: Stays polite and low-key on purpose - most people back off here, and starting loud burns the escalation you may need for someone who doesn't.

situation: Same person still won't leave - step two, dropping politeness
say: मैंने कहा न, दूर हटिए, मुझे परेशान मत कीजिए।
roman: Maine kaha na, door hatiye, mujhe pareshaan mat kijiye.
means: I already said, move away, stop bothering me.
why: Drops softening words and names the behaviour directly as harassment - the register change itself signals to onlookers that this has gone past a normal exchange.

situation: Still not leaving - step three, loud and aimed at drawing bystanders
say: ये आदमी मुझे तंग कर रहा है, कोई मदद करो!
roman: Ye aadmi mujhe tang kar raha hai, koi madad karo!
means: This man is harassing me, someone help!
why: Built to work in an Indian public space specifically - bystanders are the actual safety mechanism, not response time, so this line's job is to recruit the crowd, not just express distress.

situation: Pointing him out directly to pull a shopkeeper or crowd's attention onto him
say: ये देखिए, ये मुझे परेशान कर रहा है!
roman: Ye dekhiye, ye mujhe pareshaan kar raha hai!
means: Look at this, he is harassing me!
why: Ye dekhiye is an instruction to actually turn and look, converting nearby people from passive listeners into witnesses, which is what changes his behaviour.

situation: Asking where the bus to Ajmer leaves from
say: अजमेर की बस कहाँ से मिलेगी?
roman: Ajmer ki bus kahan se milegi?
means: From where will I get the bus to Ajmer?
why: Pushkar-Ajmer buses and shared jeeps leave from a specific stand, not a general stop - asking where you'll get it, not where the bus stop is, gets you pointed at the actual departure point.

situation: Asking when the last bus to Ajmer leaves
say: आखिरी बस कितने बजे है अजमेर की?
roman: Aakhri bus kitne baje hai Ajmer ki?
means: What time is the last bus to Ajmer?
why: Asking for the aakhri bus (last bus) specifically gets the one number that actually matters for a same-day return, instead of a full schedule you then have to parse yourself.

situation: Asking how long the road journey to Ajmer takes
say: अजमेर पहुँचने में कितना टाइम लगेगा?
roman: Ajmer pahunchne mein kitna time lagega?
means: How much time will it take to reach Ajmer?
why: The road distance itself is short, but shared transport often waits to fill up before leaving - asking travel time separately from departure time catches that gap.

situation: Confirming a hired driver or auto will wait at Ajmer while you visit the dargah
say: आप यहीं रुकेंगे न, मैं दर्शन करके आती हूँ।
roman: Aap yahin rukenge na, main darshan karke aati hoon.
means: You'll wait right here, won't you, I'll come back after visiting.
why: Phrased as confirming an assumed fact rather than asking permission - it's harder for a driver to quietly leave once he's verbally agreed to a stated plan than to a vague request.

situation: Fixing the waiting charge for a driver's wait time, before he agrees to wait
say: इंतज़ार का अलग से कितना लगेगा, अभी बता दीजिए।
roman: Intezaar ka alag se kitna lagega, abhi bata dijiye.
means: How much extra for the waiting, tell me now.
why: Same principle as the camel ride - fix the number before the wait happens, since a driver who's already waited an hour has all the leverage to name any figure.

situation: Buying a bus ticket at the counter or from the conductor
say: अजमेर का एक टिकट दीजिए।
roman: Ajmer ka ek ticket dijiye.
means: Give me one ticket to Ajmer.
why: Minimal, standard phrasing - conductors on this short route handle dozens of these a day and don't need more than this to process it.

situation: Buying a train ticket, asking about the next departure
say: अजमेर के लिए अगली ट्रेन कब है, और टिकट कहाँ मिलेगा?
roman: Ajmer ke liye agli train kab hai, aur ticket kahan milega?
means: When is the next train to Ajmer, and where do I get the ticket?
why: Bundles both questions since the same counter usually answers both - asking separately just means standing in the same line twice at a small station.

situation: Asking a temple's darshan timings
say: मंदिर के दर्शन का समय क्या है?
roman: Mandir ke darshan ka samay kya hai?
means: What is the darshan (viewing) time of the temple?
why: Darshan ka samay is the phrase temples themselves use on their own noticeboards, matching what priests and staff expect, unlike a generic 'opening time' which sounds like you're asking about a shop.

situation: Checking whether a temple someone claims is closed is actually closed
say: सच में बंद है, या अभी थोड़ी देर बाद खुलेगा?
roman: Sach mein band hai, ya abhi thodi der baad khulega?
means: Is it really closed, or will it open again shortly?
why: Directly questions the claim instead of accepting it - at high-traffic spots like the Brahma temple, a 'band hai' from a bystander sometimes precedes an offer to help you in some other paid way, so pushing back once is worth it.

situation: Asking about a temple's midday closing gap before evening aarti
say: दोपहर में कब बंद होता है और शाम को कब खुलता है?
roman: Dopahar mein kab band hota hai aur shaam ko kab khulta hai?
means: When does it close at midday and when does it reopen in the evening?
why: Most Rajasthani temples close for a midday gap and reopen for evening aarti - asking both edges of that gap in one question avoids arriving twice at the wrong time.

situation: Buying rose products (gulkand, rose water, ittar) and checking if it's really rose-based
say: ये असली गुलाब का है, या इसमें कुछ मिला हुआ है?
roman: Ye asli gulaab ka hai, ya isme kuchh mila hua hai?
means: Is this made of real rose, or is something mixed into it?
why: Naming mila hua (adulterated) directly is the question that separates Pushkar's actual farm-sourced rose stock from synthetic-scented filler sold alongside it.

situation: Checking silver purity before buying jewellery
say: ये चांदी कितने प्रतिशत शुद्ध है, हॉलमार्क है क्या इसपर?
roman: Ye chaandi kitne pratishat shuddh hai, hallmark hai kya ispar?
means: How many percent pure is this silver, does it have a hallmark on it?
why: Asking for a hallmark by name forces a real, physically checkable answer rather than a verbal purity claim you can't verify on the spot.

situation: Shopkeeper claims the silver is pure but shows no hallmark
say: बिना हॉलमार्क के मैं भरोसा नहीं करूँगी, दिखाइए कहाँ लिखा है।
roman: Bina hallmark ke main bharosa nahi karoongi, dikhaiye kahan likha hai.
means: Without a hallmark I won't trust it, show me where it's marked.
why: Demands physical proof instead of accepting reassurance, which makes an unmarked claim visibly fall apart in the conversation itself.

situation: Asking for the nearest pharmacy
say: यहाँ पास में कोई मेडिकल स्टोर है क्या?
roman: Yahan paas mein koi medical store hai kya?
means: Is there a medical store (pharmacy) nearby?
why: 'Medical store' used as-is is the actual working term across Rajasthan for a pharmacy, and gets a faster, clearer response than a more literal translation.

situation: Asking for a headache tablet
say: सर दर्द की कोई गोली मिलेगी?
roman: Sar dard ki koi goli milegi?
means: Will I get some tablet for a headache?
why: Goli (tablet) is the working word any pharmacist recognizes instantly, more specific about form than the vaguer 'dawaai'.

situation: Asking for something for stomach upset
say: पेट खराब है, कुछ दवा दीजिए।
roman: Pet kharaab hai, kuchh dawa dijiye.
means: My stomach is upset, give me some medicine.
why: Pet kharaab is the exact colloquial phrase understood immediately without describing symptoms further, and typically gets an ORS-plus-antacid combo without more questions.

situation: Asking for sanitary pads discreetly but clearly
say: सैनिटरी पैड्स मिलेंगे क्या?
roman: Sanitary pads milenge kya?
means: Will I get sanitary pads?
why: Asked plainly and directly - most medical stores keep these behind the counter and hand them over quickly, often already bagged, which matches the local norm around discretion.

situation: Asking for rehydration salts after getting dehydrated in Rajasthan's dry heat
say: गर्मी में पानी की कमी हो गई है, ORS का पैकेट दीजिए।
roman: Garmi mein paani ki kami ho gayi hai, ORS ka packet dijiye.
means: I've gotten dehydrated in the heat, give me a packet of ORS.
why: Naming ORS directly, widely recognized by that acronym even in small-town pharmacies, gets you actual rehydration salts rather than just a bottle of water, which doesn't replace lost electrolytes.

situation: Recognizing round numbers by tens when a vendor quotes a price
say: दस, बीस, तीस, चालीस, पचास, साठ, सत्तर, अस्सी, नब्बे, सौ।
roman: Das, bees, tees, chaalis, pachaas, saath, sattar, assi, nabbe, sau.
why: These are irregular words, not built from a repeating pattern the way English 'twenty, thirty, forty' are - each has to be recognized on its own, and market prices are always spoken this way, never as digits.

situation: A vendor quotes a price using dedh, dhaai or saadhe instead of a plain number
roman: Dedh sau maane 150, dhaai sau maane 250, saadhe teen sau maane 350.
means: Dedh sau means 150, dhaai sau means 250, saadhe teen sau means 350.
why: Dedh (one-and-a-half) and dhaai (two-and-a-half) are fixed irregular words, not built from 'sau' plus 'half' the way you'd guess - mishearing dedh as do (two) is a real fifty-or-hundred-rupee mistake mid-bargain.

situation: A vendor uses saadhe with a bigger base number, for a higher-value item
say: साढ़े सात सौ माने 750, साढ़े चार हज़ार माने 4500।
roman: Saadhe saat sau maane 750, saadhe chaar hazaar maane 4500.
means: Saadhe saat sau means 750, saadhe chaar hazaar means 4500.
why: Saadhe (and-a-half) attaches to any base number three and above - once this pattern is known, any half-price quote at any scale becomes decodable on the spot, not just in the hundreds.

situation: Pricing a bigger-ticket item like a rug or leather bag, quoted in thousands
roman: Hazaar maane 1000, do hazaar maane 2000, dhaai hazaar maane 2500, paanch hazaar maane 5000.
means: Hazaar means 1000, do hazaar means 2000, dhaai hazaar means 2500, paanch hazaar means 5000.
why: The same dhaai (two-and-a-half) irregular form reappears at the thousand scale, which is worth knowing once because it recurs at every order of magnitude.

situation: A vendor uses sawa, meaning a quarter more than the stated number
roman: Sawa sau maane 125, sawa do sau maane 225.
means: Sawa sau means 125, sawa do sau means 225.
why: Sawa adds a quarter to the number named - it comes up in both prices and times ('sawa char baje' is 4:15), so it's worth locking in as its own pattern rather than as a one-off price quirk.

situation: A vendor uses paune, meaning a quarter less than the next round number
roman: Paune sau maane 75, paune do sau maane 175, paune hazaar maane 750.
means: Paune sau means 75, paune do sau means 175, paune hazaar means 750.
why: Paune always counts down from the NEXT round number, the opposite direction from sawa - paune sau is a quarter short of 100, not a quarter more than anything, which is the part that trips people up first hearing it.

situation: Hearing the traditional Rajasthani greeting used by shopkeepers, hoteliers and older locals in Pushkar and Ajmer
say: खम्मा घणी
roman: Khamma ghani
means: Roughly 'my respects/salutations to you' - the standard Marwari greeting, used both on meeting and as a warm welcome.
why: Using it back, instead of a Hindi namaste, signals you recognize the local register rather than treating the person as a generic tourist-facing service - it often gets a warmer, less transactional response.

situation: Seeing the Rajasthan tourism welcome phrase on signage, or hearing a local invite you in warmly
say: पधारो म्हारे देश
roman: Padharo mhare desh
means: Come, welcome to my land - a hospitality phrase, not literal geography.
why: This is Rajasthan's own tourism slogan and a genuinely local construction - 'mhare' (my/our) and 'padharo' (come/welcome) are both Marwari forms, distinct from Hindi 'mera desh' and 'aaiye'.
src: General/training knowledge (widely used as the official Rajasthan tourism slogan); not independently confirmed via a live source this session.

situation: Hearing 'sa' added after a name or greeting by an older or rural Rajasthani speaker
say: राम राम सा
roman: Ram Ram sa
means: A respectful rural greeting - 'sa' is an honorific suffix, similar in function to 'ji' in standard Hindi.
why: Hearing 'sa' tacked onto names or greetings is a marker you're in a Marwari-speaking register, not standard Hindi - it doesn't require a special response, but recognizing it stops it sounding like a mistake or a nickname.

situation: Understanding 'mhara/mhare' when a local refers to their own family, shop or village
say: म्हारो / म्हारे
roman: Mharo / mhare
means: My / our - the Marwari equivalent of Hindi 'mera/mere'.
why: This possessive swap is one of the most common tells that someone has switched into Marwari mid-sentence even while otherwise speaking Hindi to you - useful to recognize even if you don't use it yourself.

situation: Understanding 'thaaro/thaari' when a local asks about something of yours
say: थारो / थारी
roman: Tharo / thaari
means: Your / yours - the Marwari equivalent of Hindi 'tumhara/tumhari'.
why: Pairs with mharo/mhare as the other half of the same possessive pattern - recognizing both means you're not lost when a conversation slips fully into Marwari for a sentence or two.

situation: Being asked 'kathe' when someone wants to know where you're going or where something is
say: कठे
roman: Kathe
means: Where - the Marwari equivalent of Hindi 'kahan'.
why: A short, common question word that marks Marwari speech clearly - useful to recognize since it can otherwise sound like a mumbled or unclear 'kahan'.

situation: Being asked or overhearing 'baisa' used to address a woman respectfully
say: बाईसा
roman: Baisa
means: A respectful form of address for a woman, historically used for women of standing, now used more broadly as a polite honorific.
why: If a shopkeeper or elder calls you 'baisa' instead of the Hindi 'madam' or 'behenji', it's a marker of local courtesy, not overfamiliarity - worth recognizing so it doesn't read as odd.

situation: How a Rajasthani greeting actually changes the interaction compared to a standard Hindi namaste
say: खम्मा घणी (के जवाब में सामने वाला अक्सर ज़्यादा खुल जाता है, सिर्फ़ 'नमस्ते' कहने पर उतना नहीं)
roman: Khamma ghani (ke jawaab mein saamne waala aksar zyada khul jaata hai, sirf 'namaste' kehne par utna nahi)
means: In response to khamma ghani, the other person often opens up more than a plain namaste gets you.
why: A Hindi namaste marks you as a generic North Indian visitor; a Marwari greeting marks you as someone who's made an effort with the actual local culture, and that distinction is what shifts a shopkeeper, priest or driver from transactional mode to a warmer, more generous one - worth using deliberately, not just as trivia.
